p: The Samnites were a confederation of four tribes living in the mountains east of Campania. Rome and the Samnites made a treaty in 354 BCE whose terms are not recorded; modern historians have proposed that it made the River Liris the boundary between their spheres. Livy, the only continuous source for the first war, says it began when the Samnites attacked the Sidicini and then the Campanians, and Capua surrendered itself to Rome. Modern historians doubt his three Roman victories of 343 BCE. The war ended in 341 BCE in a negotiated peace: Rome accepted that the Sidicini lay in the Samnite sphere but kept its alliance with the Campanians.

The second war grew out of Roman moves in Campania: a colony founded at Fregellae in 328 BCE and the taking of Naples in 326 BCE. In 321 BCE the consuls Titus Veturius Calvinus and Spurius Postumius Albinus were trapped by the Samnite commander Gaius Pontius in the Caudine Forks and surrendered; their soldiers passed unarmed under the yoke and six hundred equites were given as hostages. Livy says Rome rejected the agreement and avenged it, a claim some modern scholars doubt. Fighting resumed in 316 BCE, and in 304 BCE, after the fall of Bovianum, the Samnites sought peace; Livy says the old treaty was restored.

The third war began in 298 BCE, when the Lucanians asked for Roman protection against Samnite invasion. In 295 BCE Rome faced a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senone Gauls. At Sentinum the consul Publius Decius Mus devoted himself, charging into the enemy line to his death, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus won the battle; Livy gives 8,700 Roman dead and 20,000 of the enemy. Livy's surviving narrative ends in 293 BCE, and the last campaigns to 290 BCE are known only in outline.

The Samnites were forced to become allies of Rome, on terms that must have been unequal, and a colony was planted at Venusia in south-eastern Samnia. Gaius Pontius was captured, paraded in a triumph and beheaded. Around Samnia Rome had already bound the Marsi, Marrucini, Paeligni and Frentani by alliance in 304 BCE and the Vestini in 302 BCE, and it annexed the Hernici and the Sabines by giving them citizenship without the vote. The allies supplied soldiers at their own expense and shared the spoils, which greatly enlarged the manpower Rome could call on.

notes: Read in excerpts (the article has 14,700 words). The year of the fall of Bovianum is not stated in what I read (it stands just before the peace of 304 BCE); I wrote 'after the fall of Bovianum'.

The names Publius Decius Mus and Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus: the Sentinum section calls them 'Publius Decius' and 'Quintus Fabius'; the full forms occur elsewhere in the article (the military tribune of 343 BCE is also a Publius Decius Mus, and Rullianus is named as Gurges's father). The editor should confirm the consul of 295 is meant by those full names.
'Some modern scholars doubt': the article cites Salmon, who thinks the truce came from the Caudine agreement itself.
The Aurunci, named in the entry, appear in the article only before the second war (337-335 BCE).
